short: The largest of Rome's imperial bath complexes, built by the Tetrarchy to serve up to 3,000 bathers.
full:
Maximian commissioned the baths on Rome's Viminal and Quirinal hills in 298 CE in the name of his co-emperor Diocletian, and construction continued after both men abdicated in 305 until dedication in 305 or 306, completed under Constantius I. Larger than the Baths of Caracalla built a century earlier, the complex covered some 13 hectares and could accommodate an estimated 3,000 bathers at once, drawing on a purpose-built branch of the Aqua Marcia to supply its pools.

The layout followed the established sequence of cold, warm and hot rooms around a vast central hall, surrounded by gardens, libraries and lecture halls in an outer enclosure, all built at speed using the huge conscripted labour force the Tetrarchy could command. The building outlasted the western empire in continuous use and survived largely intact; Michelangelo later converted its central hall into the church of Santa Maria degli Angeli e dei Martiri, and part of the complex now houses the Museo Nazionale Romano.
